units.excerpt: In September 2023, we released our Responsible Scaling Policy (RSP), a public commitment not to train or deploy models capable of causing catastrophic harm unless we have implemented safety and security measures that will keep risks below acceptable levels.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic states that in September 2023 it released the RSP, a public commitment to avoid training or deploying catastrophically harmful models absent adequate safety and security measures.

units.excerpt: We are now updating our RSP to account for the lessons we've learned over the last year.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic notes it is updating the RSP based on lessons learned over the past year.

units.excerpt: This updated policy reflects our view that risk governance in this rapidly evolving domain should be proportional, iterative, and exportable.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic frames its updated risk governance approach as proportional, iterative, and exportable.

units.excerpt: Background. AI Safety Level Standards (ASL Standards) are a set of technical and operational measures for safely training and deploying frontier AI models.
units.paraphrase: ASL Standards are defined as technical and operational measures for safe training and deployment of frontier AI models.

units.excerpt: These currently fall into two categories: Deployment Standards and Security Standards.
units.paraphrase: ASL Standards are divided into Deployment Standards and Security Standards.

units.excerpt: As model capabilities increase, so will the need for stronger safeguards, which are captured in successively higher ASL Standards.
units.paraphrase: Stronger safeguards, reflected in higher ASL Standards, will be needed as model capabilities increase.

units.excerpt: At present, all of our models must meet the ASL-2 Deployment and Security Standards.
units.paraphrase: All current models are required to meet the ASL-2 Deployment and Security Standards.

units.excerpt: To determine when a model has become sufficiently advanced such that its deployment and security measures should be strengthened, we use the concepts of Capability Thresholds and Required Safeguards.
units.paraphrase: Capability Thresholds and Required Safeguards are the concepts used to decide when to strengthen deployment and security measures.

units.excerpt: A Capability Threshold tells us when we need to upgrade our protections, and the corresponding Required Safeguards tell us what standard should apply.
units.paraphrase: A Capability Threshold indicates timing for upgrading protections, while Required Safeguards indicate which standard applies.

units.excerpt: Capability Thresholds and Required Safeguards. The Required Safeguards for each Capability Threshold are intended to mitigate risk to acceptable levels.
units.paraphrase: Required Safeguards for each Capability Threshold aim to mitigate risk to acceptable levels.

units.excerpt: This update to our RSP provides specifications for Capabilities Thresholds related to Chemical, Biological, Radiological, and Nuclear (CBRN) weapons and Autonomous AI Research and Development (AI R&D) and identifies the corresponding Required Safeguards.
units.paraphrase: The updated RSP specifies Capability Thresholds for CBRN weapons and Autonomous AI R&D, along with their corresponding Required Safeguards.

units.excerpt: Capability assessment. We will routinely test models to determine whether their capabilities fall sufficiently far below the Capability Thresholds such that the ASL-2 Standard remains appropriate.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic commits to routinely testing models to check whether ASL-2 remains sufficient.

units.excerpt: We will first conduct preliminary assessments to determine whether a more comprehensive evaluation is needed.
units.paraphrase: Preliminary assessments will be conducted first to determine the need for comprehensive evaluation.

units.excerpt: For models requiring comprehensive testing, we will assess whether the model is unlikely to reach any relevant Capability Thresholds absent surprising advances in widely accessible post-training enhancements.
units.paraphrase: For models needing comprehensive testing, Anthropic will assess whether the model is unlikely to reach relevant Capability Thresholds barring unexpected advances in accessible post-training techniques.

units.excerpt: If, after the comprehensive testing, we determine that the model is sufficiently below the relevant Capability Thresholds, then we will continue to apply the ASL-2 Standard.
units.paraphrase: If comprehensive testing shows the model is sufficiently below the thresholds, ASL-2 continues to apply.

units.excerpt: If, however, we are unable to make the required showing, we will act as though the model has surpassed the Capability Threshold.
units.paraphrase: If the required showing cannot be made, Anthropic will treat the model as having surpassed the Capability Threshold.

units.excerpt: This means that we will both upgrade to the ASL-3 Required Safeguards and conduct a follow-up capability assessment to confirm that the ASL-4 Standard is not necessary.
units.paraphrase: Treating the model as having surpassed the threshold triggers both an upgrade to ASL-3 Required Safeguards and a follow-up assessment to rule out the need for ASL-4.

units.excerpt: Safeguards assessment. To determine whether the measures we have adopted satisfy the ASL-3 Required Safeguards, we will conduct a safeguards assessment.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic will conduct a safeguards assessment to check whether adopted measures satisfy ASL-3 Required Safeguards.

units.excerpt: For the ASL-3 Deployment Standard, we will evaluate whether it is robust to persistent attempts to misuse the capability in question.
units.paraphrase: The ASL-3 Deployment Standard evaluation checks robustness against persistent misuse attempts.

units.excerpt: For the ASL-3 Security Standard, we will evaluate whether it is highly protected against non-state attackers attempting to steal model weights.
units.paraphrase: The ASL-3 Security Standard evaluation checks protection against non-state actors attempting weight theft.

units.excerpt: If we determine that we have met the ASL-3 Required Safeguards, then we will proceed to deployment, provided we have also conducted a follow-up capability assessment.
units.paraphrase: Deployment proceeds once ASL-3 Required Safeguards are met and a follow-up capability assessment has been conducted.

units.excerpt: Follow-up capability assessment. In parallel with upgrading a model to the ASL-3 Required Safeguards, we will conduct a follow-up capability assessment to confirm that further safeguards are not necessary.
units.paraphrase: While upgrading to ASL-3 Required Safeguards, a follow-up capability assessment will confirm whether further safeguards are needed.

units.excerpt: Deployment and scaling outcomes. We may deploy or store a model if either of the following criteria are met: (1) the model's capabilities are sufficiently far away from the existing Capability Thresholds, making the current ASL-2 Standard appropriate;
units.paraphrase: A model may be deployed or stored if its capabilities are sufficiently far from existing Capability Thresholds, keeping ASL-2 appropriate.

units.context_stem: We may deploy or store a model if either of the following criteria are met
units.excerpt: or (2) the model's capabilities have surpassed the existing Capabilities Threshold, but we have implemented the ASL-3 Required Safeguards and conducted the follow-up capability assessment.
units.paraphrase: Alternatively, a model may be deployed or stored if it has surpassed the Capability Threshold but ASL-3 Required Safeguards and a follow-up assessment are in place.

units.excerpt: In any scenario where we determine that a model requires ASL-3 Required Safeguards but we are unable to implement them immediately, we will act promptly to reduce interim risk to acceptable levels until the ASL-3 Required Safeguards are in place.
units.paraphrase: If ASL-3 Required Safeguards cannot be implemented immediately, Anthropic commits to promptly reducing interim risk until they are in place.

units.excerpt: Governance and transparency. To facilitate the effective implementation of this policy across the company, we commit to several internal governance measures, including maintaining the position of Responsible Scaling Officer, establishing a process through which Anthropic staff may anonymously notify the Responsible Scaling Officer of any potential instances of noncompliance, and developing internal safety procedures for incident scenarios.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic commits to internal governance measures including a Responsible Scaling Officer role, an anonymous noncompliance reporting channel, and internal incident procedures.

units.excerpt: To advance the public dialogue on the regulation of frontier AI model risks and to enable examination of our actions, we will also publicly release key materials related to the evaluation and deployment of our models with sensitive information removed and solicit input from external experts in relevant domains.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic commits to publicly releasing evaluation and deployment materials, redacted of sensitive information, and to seeking external expert input.

units.excerpt: As frontier AI models advance, we believe they will bring about transformative benefits for our society and economy.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic states its belief that advancing frontier AI models will bring transformative societal and economic benefits.

units.excerpt: AI could accelerate scientific discoveries, revolutionize healthcare, enhance our education system, and create entirely new domains for human creativity and innovation.
units.paraphrase: AI is described as potentially accelerating science, healthcare, education, and creativity.

units.excerpt: Frontier AI models also, however, present new challenges and risks that warrant careful study and effective safeguards.
units.paraphrase: Frontier AI models also pose new risks requiring careful study and effective safeguards.

units.excerpt: In September 2023, we released our Responsible Scaling Policy (RSP), a first-of-its-kind public commitment not to train or deploy models capable of causing catastrophic harm unless we have implemented safety and security measures that will keep risks below acceptable levels.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic reiterates the original 2023 RSP commitment against training or deploying catastrophically dangerous models without adequate safety and security measures.

units.excerpt: Our RSP serves several purposes: it is an internal operating procedure for investigating and mitigating these risks and helps inform the public of our plans and commitments.
units.paraphrase: The RSP serves as both an internal operating procedure and a public communication of Anthropic's plans and commitments.

units.excerpt: We also hope it will serve as a prototype for other companies looking to adopt similar frameworks and, potentially, inform regulators about possible best practices.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic hopes the RSP can serve as a model for other companies and inform regulatory best practices.

units.excerpt: We are now updating our RSP to account for the lessons we've learned over the last year.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic reiterates that the RSP is being updated based on lessons learned.

units.excerpt: This policy reflects our view that risk governance in this rapidly evolving domain should be proportional, iterative, and exportable.
units.paraphrase: The policy reflects the view that risk governance should be proportional, iterative, and exportable.

units.excerpt: First, our approach to risk should be proportional. Central to our policy is the concept of AI Safety Level Standards: technical and operational standards for safely training and deploying frontier models that correspond with a particular level of risk.
units.paraphrase: The proportionality principle centers on AI Safety Level Standards that scale with the level of risk posed by a model.

units.excerpt: By implementing safeguards that are proportional to the nature and extent of an AI model's risks, we can balance innovation with safety, maintaining rigorous protections without unnecessarily hindering progress.
units.paraphrase: Proportional safeguards are intended to balance safety and innovation without unnecessary hindrance.

units.excerpt: This approach also enables us to allocate resources efficiently, focusing our most stringent safeguards on the models that pose the greater risk, while affording more flexibility for lower-risk systems.
units.paraphrase: The proportional approach lets Anthropic focus stringent safeguards on higher-risk models and allow flexibility for lower-risk systems.

units.excerpt: Second, our approach to risk should be iterative. Since the frontier of AI is rapidly evolving, we cannot anticipate what safety and security measures will be appropriate for models far beyond the current frontier.
units.paraphrase: The iterative principle acknowledges that future safety measures cannot be fully anticipated given rapid AI progress.

units.excerpt: We will thus regularly measure the capability of our models and adjust our safeguards accordingly.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic will regularly measure model capability and adjust safeguards accordingly.

units.excerpt: Further, we will continue to research potential risks and next-generation mitigation techniques.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic will continue researching potential risks and future mitigation techniques.

units.excerpt: And, at the highest level of generality, we will look for opportunities to improve and strengthen our overarching risk management framework.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic will seek opportunities to strengthen its overall risk management framework.

units.excerpt: Third, our approach to risk should be exportable. To demonstrate that it is possible to balance innovation with safety, we must put forward our proof of concept: a pragmatic, flexible, and scalable approach to risk governance.
units.paraphrase: The exportability principle involves presenting a pragmatic, scalable risk governance model as proof that innovation and safety can coexist.

units.excerpt: By sharing our approach externally, we aim to set a new industry standard that encourages widespread adoption of similar frameworks.
units.paraphrase: Sharing the approach externally aims to set an industry standard encouraging wider adoption.

units.excerpt: In the long term, we hope that our policy may offer relevant insights for regulation.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic hopes the policy could inform future regulation over the long term.

units.excerpt: In the meantime, we will continue to share our findings with policymakers.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic will continue sharing findings with policymakers in the interim.

units.excerpt: Although this policy focuses on catastrophic risks, they are not the only risks that we consider important.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic notes that catastrophic risks are the focus of this policy but not the only risks it considers important.

units.excerpt: Our Usage Policy sets forth our standards for the use of our products, including prohibitions on using our models to spread misinformation, incite violence or hateful behavior, or engage in fraudulent or abusive practices, and we continually refine our technical measures for enforcing our trust and safety standards at scale.
units.paraphrase: The separate Usage Policy prohibits misuse such as misinformation, incitement, and fraud, and Anthropic continually refines enforcement measures.

units.excerpt: Further, we conduct research to understand the broader societal impacts of our models.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic conducts research into broader societal impacts of its models.

units.excerpt: Our Responsible Scaling Policy complements our work in these areas, contributing to our understanding of current and potential risks.
units.paraphrase: The RSP is described as complementary to other risk-related work at Anthropic.

units.excerpt: At Anthropic, we are committed to developing AI responsibly and transparently.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic states its commitment to responsible and transparent AI development.

units.excerpt: Since our founding, we have recognized the importance of proactively addressing potential risks as we push the boundaries of AI capability and of clearly communicating about the nature and extent of those risks.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic states it has long recognized the importance of proactive risk management and clear communication about risk.

units.excerpt: We look forward to continuing to refine our approach to risk governance and to collaborating with stakeholders across the AI ecosystem.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic expresses intent to keep refining its risk governance and to collaborate with ecosystem stakeholders.

units.excerpt: This policy is designed in the spirit of the Responsible Scaling Policy (RSP) framework introduced by the non-profit AI safety organization METR, as well as emerging government policy proposals in the UK, EU, and US.
units.paraphrase: The policy is framed as inspired by METR's RSP framework and emerging UK, EU, and US government policy proposals.

units.excerpt: This policy also helps satisfy our Voluntary White House Commitments (2023) and Frontier AI Safety Commitments (2024).
units.paraphrase: The policy is also said to help satisfy the 2023 Voluntary White House Commitments and 2024 Frontier AI Safety Commitments.

units.excerpt: We extend our sincere gratitude to the many external groups that provided invaluable guidance on the development and refinement of our Responsible Scaling Policy.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic thanks external groups for input on developing the RSP.

units.excerpt: We actively welcome feedback on our policy and suggestions for improvement from other entities engaged in frontier AI risk evaluations or safety and security standards.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic invites feedback from other organizations working on frontier AI risk and safety standards.

units.excerpt: To submit your feedback or suggestions, please contact us at rsp@anthropic.com.
units.paraphrase: Feedback and suggestions can be submitted to a provided contact email.

units.excerpt: AI Safety Level Standards (ASL Standards) are core to our risk mitigation strategy. An ASL Standard is a set of technical and operational measures for safely training and deploying frontier AI models.
units.paraphrase: ASL Standards are core to Anthropic's risk mitigation and are defined as technical and operational measures for safe training and deployment.

units.excerpt: As model capabilities increase, so will the need for stronger safeguards, which are captured in successively higher ASL Standards.
units.paraphrase: Higher capabilities require stronger safeguards, reflected in successively higher ASL Standards.

units.excerpt: Definitions of ASL Standards and other key terms are available in Appendix A.
units.paraphrase: Appendix A contains definitions of ASL Standards and other key terms.

units.excerpt: The types of measures that compose an ASL Standard currently fall into two categories–Deployment Standards and Security Standards–which map onto the types of risks that frontier AI models may pose.
units.paraphrase: ASL Standards consist of Deployment Standards and Security Standards, each mapping onto different risk types.

units.excerpt: Deployment Standards: Deployment Standards are technical, operational, and policy measures to ensure the safe usage of AI models by external users (i.e., our users and customers) as well as internal users (i.e., our employees).
units.paraphrase: Deployment Standards are defined as measures ensuring safe use of AI models by both external and internal users.

units.excerpt: Deployment Standards aim to strike a balance between enabling beneficial use of AI technologies and mitigating the risks of potentially catastrophic cases of misuse.
units.paraphrase: Deployment Standards seek to balance beneficial use against catastrophic misuse risk.

units.excerpt: Security Standards: Security Standards are technical, operational, and policy measures to protect AI models–particularly their weights and associated systems–from unauthorized access, theft, or compromise by malicious actors.
units.paraphrase: Security Standards are defined as measures protecting AI models, especially weights, from unauthorized access or theft.

units.excerpt: Security Standards are intended to maintain the integrity and controlled use of AI models throughout their lifecycle, from development to deployment.
units.paraphrase: Security Standards aim to preserve model integrity and controlled use across the model lifecycle.

units.excerpt: We expect to continue refining our framework in response to future risks (for example, the risk that an AI system attempts to subvert the goals of its operators).
units.paraphrase: Anthropic expects to keep refining its framework to address future risks such as an AI subverting operator goals.

units.excerpt: At present, all of our models must meet the ASL-2 Deployment and Security Standards. The ASL-2 Security and Deployment Standards provide a baseline level of safe deployment and model security for AI models.
units.paraphrase: All current models must meet ASL-2 standards, which provide baseline safety and security.

units.excerpt: These standards, which are summarized below, are available in full in Appendix B.
units.paraphrase: The full ASL-2 standards are located in Appendix B, with a summary given here.

units.excerpt: The ASL-2 Deployment Standard reduces the prevalence of misuse, and includes the publication of model cards and enforcement of Usage Policy; harmlessness training such as Constitutional AI and automated detection mechanisms; and establishing vulnerability reporting channels as well as a bug bounty for universal jailbreaks.
units.paraphrase: ASL-2 Deployment Standard includes model card publication, Usage Policy enforcement, harmlessness training, detection mechanisms, vulnerability reporting, and a jailbreak bug bounty.

units.excerpt: The ASL-2 Security Standard requires a security system that can likely thwart most opportunistic attackers and includes vendor and supplier security reviews, physical security measures, and the use of secure-by-design principles.
units.paraphrase: ASL-2 Security Standard requires defenses against most opportunistic attackers, plus vendor reviews, physical security, and secure-by-design practices.

units.excerpt: Although the ASL-2 Standard is appropriate for all of our current models, that may not hold true in the future as our models become more capable.
units.paraphrase: ASL-2 is currently sufficient but may not remain so as models grow more capable.

units.excerpt: To determine when a model has become sufficiently advanced such that its deployment and security measures should be strengthened, we use the concepts of Capability Thresholds and Required Safeguards.
units.paraphrase: Capability Thresholds and Required Safeguards determine when safeguards should be strengthened.

units.excerpt: A Capability Threshold tells us when we need to upgrade our protections, and the corresponding Required Safeguards tell us what standard should apply.
units.paraphrase: A Capability Threshold signals timing for upgrading protections; Required Safeguards specify which standard applies.

units.excerpt: A Capability Threshold is a prespecified level of AI capability that, if reached, signals (1) a meaningful increase in the level of risk if the model remains under the existing set of safeguards and (2) a corresponding need to upgrade the safeguards to a higher ASL Standard.
units.paraphrase: A Capability Threshold is defined as a preset capability level signaling both increased risk and a need for higher safeguards.

units.excerpt: In other words, a Capability Threshold serves as a trigger for shifting from an ASL-N Standard to an ASL-N+1 Standard (or, in some cases, moving straight to ASL N+2 or higher).
units.paraphrase: A Capability Threshold triggers a shift from one ASL Standard to the next, or occasionally a jump of more than one level.

units.excerpt: Depending on the Capability Threshold, it may not be necessary to upgrade both the Deployment and Security Standards; each Capability Threshold corresponds to specific Required Safeguards that identify which of the ASL Standards must be met.
units.paraphrase: Not every Capability Threshold requires upgrading both standards; each threshold maps to specific Required Safeguards identifying which standards apply.

units.excerpt: Below, we specify the Capability Thresholds and their corresponding Required Safeguards. The Required Safeguards for each Capability Threshold are intended to mitigate risk from a model with such capabilities to acceptable levels.
units.paraphrase: This section specifies Capability Thresholds and Required Safeguards intended to mitigate risk to acceptable levels.

units.excerpt: In developing these standards, we have weighed the risks and benefits of frontier model development.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic states it weighed risks and benefits of frontier model development in creating these standards.

units.excerpt: We believe these safeguards are achievable with sufficient investment and advance planning into research and development and would advocate for the industry as a whole to adopt them.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic believes the safeguards are achievable with investment and planning, and advocates industry-wide adoption.

units.excerpt: We will conduct assessments to inform when to implement the Required Safeguards (see Section 4).
units.paraphrase: Assessments will determine the timing for implementing Required Safeguards.

units.excerpt: The Capability Thresholds summarized below are available in full in Appendix C.
units.paraphrase: Full Capability Thresholds are located in Appendix C, summarized in the following table.

units.paraphrase: CBRN-3 threshold is defined as the ability to significantly help those with basic technical backgrounds create or deploy CBRN weapons.

units.paraphrase: The rationale states CBRN-3 capability could greatly expand the pool of dangerous actors without a corresponding defensive improvement.

units.paraphrase: CBRN-3 requires both the ASL-3 Deployment Standard and ASL-3 Security Standard, protecting against misuse and non-state weight theft.

units.paraphrase: CBRN-4 is defined as the ability to substantially uplift state-level CBRN programs through novel weapons design, acceleration, or reduced technical barriers.

units.paraphrase: CBRN-4 is expected to require ASL-4 Deployment and Security Standards, with details to be added later.

units.paraphrase: AI R&D-4 threshold is defined as the ability to fully automate an entry-level remote researcher's work at Anthropic.

units.paraphrase: AI R&D-4 requires the ASL-3 Security Standard.

units.excerpt: In addition, we will develop an affirmative case that (1) identifies the most immediate and relevant risks from models pursuing misaligned goals and (2) explains how we have mitigated these risks to acceptable levels.
units.paraphrase: For AI R&D-4, an affirmative case will be developed identifying misalignment risks and explaining their mitigation.

units.excerpt: The affirmative case will describe, as relevant, evidence on model capabilities; evidence on AI alignment; mitigations (such as monitoring and other safeguards); and our overall reasoning.
units.paraphrase: The affirmative case for AI R&D-4 will cover capability evidence, alignment evidence, mitigations, and overall reasoning.

units.excerpt: AI R&D-5: The ability to cause dramatic acceleration in the rate of effective scaling
units.paraphrase: AI R&D-5 threshold is defined as the ability to cause dramatic acceleration in effective scaling rate.

units.excerpt: At minimum, the ASL-4 Security Standard (which would protect against model-weight theft by state-level adversaries) is required, although we expect a higher security standard may be required.
units.paraphrase: AI R&D-5 requires at least the ASL-4 Security Standard, though an even higher standard may be needed.

units.excerpt: As with AI R&D-4, we also expect an affirmative case will be required.
units.paraphrase: Similar to AI R&D-4, an affirmative case is expected to be required for AI R&D-5.

units.excerpt: These Capability Thresholds represent our current understanding of the most pressing catastrophic risks.
units.paraphrase: The listed Capability Thresholds reflect Anthropic's current understanding of the most pressing catastrophic risks.

units.excerpt: As our understanding evolves, we may identify additional thresholds.
units.paraphrase: Additional thresholds may be identified as understanding evolves.

units.excerpt: For each threshold, we will identify and describe the corresponding Required Safeguards as soon as feasible, and at minimum before training or deploying any model that reaches that threshold.
units.paraphrase: Required Safeguards for each threshold will be identified as soon as feasible and no later than before training or deploying a model reaching that threshold.

units.excerpt: We will consider it sufficient to rule out the possibility that a model has surpassed the two Autonomous AI R&D Capability Thresholds by considering an earlier (i.e., less capable) checkpoint: the ability to autonomously perform a wide range of 2-8 hour software engineering tasks.
units.paraphrase: An earlier checkpoint — autonomous performance of 2-8 hour software engineering tasks — will suffice to rule out surpassing the AI R&D thresholds.

units.excerpt: We would view this level of capability as an important checkpoint towards both Autonomous AI R&D as well as other capabilities that may warrant similar attention (for example, autonomous replication).
units.paraphrase: This checkpoint capability is viewed as significant for both AI R&D and other concerning capabilities like autonomous replication.

units.excerpt: We will test for this checkpoint and, by the time we reach it, we will (1) aim to have met (or be close to meeting) the ASL-3 Security Standard as an intermediate goal;
units.paraphrase: Anthropic will test for this checkpoint and aim to have met or nearly met the ASL-3 Security Standard by that time.

units.context_stem: we will (1) aim to have met (or be close to meeting) the ASL-3 Security Standard as an intermediate goal;
units.excerpt: (2) share an update on our progress around that time; and (3) begin testing for the full Autonomous AI R&D Capability Threshold and any additional risks.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic also commits to sharing a progress update and beginning testing for the full AI R&D threshold and additional risks around that time.

units.excerpt: We will also maintain a list of capabilities that we think require significant investigation and may require stronger safeguards than ASL-2 provides.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic will maintain a watch list of capabilities that may need stronger-than-ASL-2 safeguards.

units.excerpt: This group of capabilities could pose serious risks, but the exact Capability Threshold and the Required Safeguards are not clear at present.
units.paraphrase: These capabilities could pose serious risks, though precise thresholds and safeguards are not yet defined.

units.excerpt: These capabilities may warrant a higher standard of safeguards, such as the ASL-3 Security or Deployment Standard.
units.paraphrase: These watch-list capabilities might require a higher standard such as ASL-3 Security or Deployment.

units.excerpt: However, it is also possible that by the time these capabilities are reached, there will be evidence that such a standard is not necessary (for example, because of the potential use of similar capabilities for defensive purposes).
units.paraphrase: It is also possible that evidence will eventually show a higher standard is unnecessary, for example if the capability can be used defensively.

units.excerpt: Instead of prespecifying particular thresholds and safeguards today, we will conduct ongoing assessments of the risks with the goal of determining in a future iteration of this policy what the Capability Thresholds and Required Safeguards would be.
units.paraphrase: Rather than fixing thresholds now, Anthropic will assess risks on an ongoing basis to define thresholds and safeguards in a future policy update.

units.excerpt: At present, we have identified one such capability:
units.paraphrase: Anthropic states it has currently identified one capability of this kind.

units.excerpt: Cyber Operations: The ability to significantly enhance or automate sophisticated destructive cyber attacks, including but not limited to discovering novel zero-day exploit chains, developing complex malware, or orchestrating extensive hard-to-detect network intrusions.
units.paraphrase: Cyber Operations capability is defined as significantly enhancing or automating sophisticated destructive cyber attacks, including zero-day discovery, malware development, and network intrusion.

units.context_stem: Row: Cyber Operations. Column: Ongoing Assessment.
units.excerpt: This will involve engaging with experts in cyber operations to assess the potential for frontier models to both enhance and mitigate cyber threats, and considering the implementation of tiered access controls or phased deployments for models with advanced cyber capabilities.
units.paraphrase: Ongoing assessment for Cyber Operations involves expert engagement and consideration of tiered access or phased deployment.

units.context_stem: Row: Cyber Operations. Column: Ongoing Assessment.
units.excerpt: We will conduct either pre- or post-deployment testing, including specialized evaluations.
units.paraphrase: Testing, including specialized evaluations, will occur either before or after deployment.

units.context_stem: Row: Cyber Operations. Column: Ongoing Assessment.
units.excerpt: We will document any salient results alongside our Capability Reports (see Section 3).
units.paraphrase: Salient cyber capability results will be documented alongside Capability Reports.

units.excerpt: We hope to publish updates approximately every 6 months.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic hopes to publish updates roughly every six months.

units.excerpt: Overall, our decision to prioritize the capabilities in the two tables above is based on commissioned research reports, discussions with domain experts, input from expert forecasters, public research, conversations with other industry actors through the Frontier Model Forum, and internal discussions.
units.paraphrase: The prioritized capabilities were selected based on research, expert discussions, forecaster input, public research, industry conversations via the Frontier Model Forum, and internal deliberation.

units.excerpt: As the field evolves and our understanding deepens, we remain committed to refining our approach.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic commits to continuing to refine its approach as the field and understanding evolve.

units.excerpt: We recognize the potential risks of highly persuasive AI models. While we are actively consulting experts, we believe this capability is not yet sufficiently understood to include in our current commitments.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic acknowledges persuasive AI risks but considers the capability not yet sufficiently understood to warrant inclusion in current commitments.

units.excerpt: We will routinely test models to determine whether their capabilities fall sufficiently far below the Capability Thresholds such that we are confident that the ASL-2 Standard remains appropriate.
units.paraphrase: Routine testing will confirm that models remain sufficiently below Capability Thresholds so ASL-2 remains appropriate.

units.excerpt: We will first conduct preliminary assessments (on both new and existing models, as needed) to determine whether a more comprehensive evaluation is needed.
units.paraphrase: Preliminary assessments will be conducted on new and existing models as needed to determine whether comprehensive evaluation is required.

units.excerpt: The purpose of this preliminary assessment is to identify whether the model is notably more capable than the last model that underwent a comprehensive assessment.
units.paraphrase: The preliminary assessment aims to determine whether a model is notably more capable than the last comprehensively assessed model.

units.excerpt: The term "notably more capable" is operationalized as at least one of the following:
units.paraphrase: The term "notably more capable" is defined by at least one of the listed conditions.

units.context_stem: The term "notably more capable" is operationalized as at least one of the following:
units.excerpt: The model is notably more performant on automated tests in risk-relevant domains (defined as 4x or more in Effective Compute).
units.paraphrase: One trigger for "notably more capable" is at least a 4x increase in Effective Compute-equivalent performance on risk-relevant automated tests.

units.context_stem: The term "notably more capable" is operationalized as at least one of the following:
units.excerpt: Six months' worth of finetuning and other capability elicitation methods have accumulated. This is measured in calendar time, since we do not yet have a metric to estimate the impact of these improvements more precisely.
units.paraphrase: The second trigger is six months of accumulated finetuning and elicitation methods, measured in calendar time absent a more precise metric.

units.excerpt: In addition, the Responsible Scaling Officer may in their discretion determine that a comprehensive assessment is warranted.
units.paraphrase: The Responsible Scaling Officer has discretion to determine that comprehensive assessment is warranted regardless of the standard criteria.

units.excerpt: If a new or existing model is below the "notably more capable" standard, no further testing is necessary.
units.paraphrase: No further testing is required if a model falls below the "notably more capable" standard.

units.excerpt: For models requiring comprehensive testing, we will assess whether the model is unlikely to reach any relevant Capability Thresholds absent surprising advances in widely accessible post-training enhancements.
units.paraphrase: Comprehensive testing assesses whether a model is unlikely to reach relevant Capability Thresholds barring unexpected accessible post-training advances.

units.excerpt: To make the required showing, we will need to satisfy the following criteria:
units.paraphrase: Satisfying the required showing requires meeting the following listed criteria.

units.context_stem: To make the required showing, we will need to satisfy the following criteria:
units.excerpt: Threat model mapping: For each capability threshold, make a compelling case that we have mapped out the most likely and consequential threat models: combinations of actors (if relevant), attack pathways, model capability bottlenecks, and types of harms.
units.paraphrase: Criterion one requires mapping out the most likely and consequential threat models, including actors, attack pathways, capability bottlenecks, and harm types.

units.excerpt: We also make a compelling case that there does not exist a threat model that we are not evaluating that represents a substantial amount of risk.
units.paraphrase: Criterion one also requires demonstrating that no unevaluated threat model represents substantial risk.

units.context_stem: To make the required showing, we will need to satisfy the following criteria:
units.excerpt: Evaluations: Design and run empirical tests that provide strong evidence that the model does not have the requisite skills; explain why the tests yielded such results; and check at test time that the results are attributable to the model's capabilities rather than issues with the test design.
units.paraphrase: Criterion two requires empirical tests demonstrating the model lacks requisite skills, with explanation of results and verification that they reflect model capability rather than test design flaws.

units.excerpt: Findings from partner organizations and external evaluations of our models (or similar models) should also be incorporated into the final assessment, when available.
units.paraphrase: Findings from partner organizations and external evaluations should be incorporated into the final assessment when available.

units.context_stem: To make the required showing, we will need to satisfy the following criteria:
units.excerpt: Elicitation: Demonstrate that, when given enough resources to extrapolate to realistic attackers, researchers cannot elicit sufficiently useful results from the model on the relevant tasks.
units.paraphrase: Criterion three requires demonstrating that researchers, given realistic attacker-level resources, cannot elicit sufficiently useful results from the model.

units.excerpt: We should assume that jailbreaks and model weight theft are possibilities, and therefore perform testing on models without safety mechanisms (such as harmlessness training) that could obscure these capabilities.
units.paraphrase: Testing should assume jailbreaks and weight theft are possible and be conducted on models without safety mechanisms that might mask true capabilities.

units.excerpt: We will also consider the possible performance increase from using resources that a realistic attacker would have access to, such as scaffolding, finetuning, and expert prompting.
units.paraphrase: Consideration will be given to performance gains from resources realistic attackers could access, such as scaffolding, finetuning, and expert prompting.

units.excerpt: At minimum, we will perform basic finetuning for instruction following, tool use, minimizing refusal rates.
units.paraphrase: At a minimum, basic finetuning will be performed for instruction following, tool use, and reduced refusal rates.

units.excerpt: "Effective Compute" is a scaling-trend-based metric that accounts for both FLOPs and algorithmic improvements. An Effective Compute increase of K represents a performance improvement from a pretrained model on relevant task(s) equivalent to scaling up the baseline model's training compute by a factor of K.
units.paraphrase: Effective Compute is defined as a metric combining FLOPs and algorithmic improvements, where an increase of K equals a performance gain equivalent to scaling training compute by factor K.

units.excerpt: We plan to track Effective Compute during pretraining on a weighted aggregation of datasets relevant to our Capability Thresholds (e.g., coding and science).
units.paraphrase: Effective Compute will be tracked during pretraining using a weighted aggregation of relevant datasets like coding and science.

units.excerpt: This is, however, an open research question, and we will explore different possible methods.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic acknowledges this is an open research question and will explore different methods.

units.excerpt: More generally, the Effective Compute concept is fairly new, and we may replace it with another metric in a similar spirit in the future.
units.paraphrase: The Effective Compute concept is new and may be replaced by a similar future metric.

units.excerpt: This is a broad category, including techniques like improved prompting and agent scaffolding.
units.paraphrase: The category of capability elicitation methods is broad, including improved prompting and agent scaffolding.

units.excerpt: Exploring ways to integrate these types of improvements into an overall metric is an ongoing area of research.
units.paraphrase: Integrating these improvements into an overall metric remains an ongoing research area.

units.excerpt: By "widely accessible," we mean techniques that are available to a moderately resourced group (i.e., do not involve setting up large amounts of custom infrastructure or using confidential information).
units.paraphrase: "Widely accessible" is defined as techniques available to a moderately resourced group without large custom infrastructure or confidential information.

units.excerpt: We include headroom to account for the possibility that the model is either modified via one of our own finetuning products or stolen in the months following testing, and used to create a model that has reached a Capability Threshold.
units.paraphrase: Headroom is built in to account for possible finetuning or theft after testing that could push a model to a Capability Threshold.

units.excerpt: That said, estimating these future effects is very difficult given the state of research today.
units.paraphrase: Estimating these future effects is acknowledged as very difficult given current research limitations.

units.context_stem: To make the required showing, we will need to satisfy the following criteria:
units.excerpt: Forecasting: Make informal forecasts about the likelihood that further training and elicitation will improve test results between the time of testing and the next expected round of comprehensive testing.
units.paraphrase: Criterion four requires informal forecasts of the likelihood that further training and elicitation will improve results before the next comprehensive testing round.

units.excerpt: This testing and the subsequent capability decision should ideally be concluded within about a month of reaching the "notably more capable" threshold.
units.paraphrase: Testing and the resulting capability decision should ideally conclude within about a month of reaching the "notably more capable" threshold.

units.excerpt: If, after the comprehensive testing, we determine that the model is sufficiently below the relevant Capability Thresholds, then we will continue to apply the ASL-2 Standard.
units.paraphrase: ASL-2 continues to apply if comprehensive testing shows the model is sufficiently below relevant thresholds.

units.excerpt: The process for making such a determination is as follows:
units.paraphrase: The following steps describe the determination process.

units.context_stem: The process for making such a determination is as follows:
units.excerpt: First, we will compile a Capability Report that documents the findings from the comprehensive assessment, makes an affirmative case for why the Capability Threshold is sufficiently far away, and advances recommendations on deployment decisions.
units.paraphrase: Step one requires compiling a Capability Report documenting findings, an affirmative case for distance from the threshold, and deployment recommendations.

units.context_stem: The process for making such a determination is as follows:
units.excerpt: The report will be escalated to the CEO and the Responsible Scaling Officer, who will (1) make the ultimate determination as to whether we have sufficiently established that we are unlikely to reach the Capability Threshold and (2) decide any deployment-related issues.
units.paraphrase: Step two escalates the report to the CEO and RSO, who make the final determination on threshold proximity and deployment issues.

units.context_stem: The process for making such a determination is as follows:
units.excerpt: In general, as noted in Sections 7.1.4 and 7.2.2, we will solicit both internal and external expert feedback on the report as well as the CEO and RSO's conclusions to inform future refinements to our methodology.
units.paraphrase: Step three involves generally soliciting internal and external expert feedback on the report and conclusions to inform future methodology.

units.excerpt: For high-stakes issues, however, the CEO and RSO will likely solicit internal and external feedback on the report prior to making any decisions.
units.paraphrase: For high-stakes issues, the CEO and RSO will likely solicit feedback before making decisions, rather than after.

units.context_stem: The process for making such a determination is as follows:
units.excerpt: If the CEO and RSO decide to proceed with deployment, they will share their decision–as well as the underlying Capability Report, internal feedback, and any external feedback–with the Board of Directors and the Long-Term Benefit Trust before moving forward.
units.paraphrase: Step four requires sharing the deployment decision and supporting materials with the Board of Directors and the Long-Term Benefit Trust before proceeding.

units.excerpt: If, however, we determine we are unable to make the required showing, we will act as though the model has surpassed the Capability Threshold.
units.paraphrase: If the required showing cannot be made, the model will be treated as having surpassed the Capability Threshold.

units.excerpt: This means that we will (1) upgrade to the ASL-3 Required Safeguards (see Section 4) and (2) conduct follow-up a capability assessment to confirm that the ASL-4 Standard is not necessary (see Section 5).
units.paraphrase: This triggers upgrading to ASL-3 Required Safeguards and conducting a follow-up assessment to confirm ASL-4 is unnecessary.

units.excerpt: To determine whether the measures we have adopted satisfy the ASL-3 Required Safeguards, we will conduct a safeguards assessment.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic will conduct a safeguards assessment to determine whether adopted measures satisfy the ASL-3 Required Safeguards.

units.excerpt: As noted, the Required Safeguards for each Capability Threshold are specified in Section 2.
units.paraphrase: The Required Safeguards for each Capability Threshold are specified elsewhere in Section 2.

units.excerpt: We will document our implementation of the Required Safeguards in a Safeguards Report.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic will document its implementation of the Required Safeguards in a Safeguards Report.

units.excerpt: Currently, these will be informal estimates of (1) the extent to which widely available elicitation techniques may improve and (2) how the model will perform on the same tasks when the next round of testing begins.
units.paraphrase: The footnote explains that these forecasts are currently informal estimates about elicitation technique improvement and future model performance.

units.excerpt: As these are open research questions, we will aim to improve these forecasts over time so that they can be relied upon for risk judgments.
units.paraphrase: Because these are open research questions, Anthropic aims to improve the forecasts over time for reliable risk judgments.

units.excerpt: In the case where the capability assessment shows a model is just barely below the threshold, the Responsible Scaling Officer may choose to limit further training to some amount less than the default 4x Effective Compute increase until ASL-3 measures are in place, in order to limit risk.
units.paraphrase: If a model is just barely below the threshold, the Responsible Scaling Officer may restrict further training below the default 4x Effective Compute increase until ASL-3 measures are implemented.

units.excerpt: There may be a substantial period during which models are not demonstrably close to the Capability Threshold, but we nevertheless are unable to rule out the risk to our satisfaction, and thus choose to implement the Required Safeguards.
units.paraphrase: Even when models aren't clearly close to the Capability Threshold, Anthropic may still implement Required Safeguards if risk cannot be ruled out to its satisfaction.

units.excerpt: When a model must meet the ASL-3 Deployment Standard, we will evaluate whether the measures we have implemented make us robust to persistent attempts to misuse the capability in question.
units.paraphrase: When the ASL-3 Deployment Standard applies, Anthropic will assess whether its measures make it robust against persistent misuse attempts.

units.excerpt: To make the required showing, we will need to satisfy the following criteria:
units.paraphrase: Anthropic states it must satisfy the following listed criteria to make the required showing.

units.context_stem: To make the required showing, we will need to satisfy the following criteria:
units.excerpt: Threat modeling: Make a compelling case that the set of threats and the vectors through which an adversary could catastrophically misuse the deployed system have been sufficiently mapped out, and will commit to revising as necessary over time.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic must show that threats and misuse vectors have been adequately mapped and commit to revising this over time.

units.context_stem: To make the required showing, we will need to satisfy the following criteria:
units.excerpt: Defense in depth: Use a "defense in depth" approach by building a series of defensive layers, each designed to catch misuse attempts that might pass through previous barriers.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic must build layered defenses that catch misuse attempts that slip past earlier layers.

units.excerpt: As an example, this might entail achieving a high overall recall rate using harm refusal techniques. This is an area of active research, and new technologies may be added when ready.
units.paraphrase: An example is achieving high recall via harm refusal techniques; this remains an active research area where new technologies may be added.

units.context_stem: To make the required showing, we will need to satisfy the following criteria:
units.excerpt: Red-teaming: Conduct red-teaming that demonstrates that threat actors with realistic access levels and resources are highly unlikely to be able to consistently elicit information from any generally accessible systems that greatly increases their ability to cause catastrophic harm relative to other available tools.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic must conduct red-teaming demonstrating that realistic threat actors are highly unlikely to consistently extract catastrophic-harm-enabling information beyond what other tools provide.

units.context_stem: To make the required showing, we will need to satisfy the following criteria:
units.excerpt: Rapid remediation: Show that any compromises of the deployed system, such as jailbreaks or other attack pathways, will be identified and remediated promptly enough to prevent the overall system from meaningfully increasing an adversary's ability to cause catastrophic harm.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic must demonstrate that system compromises will be identified and fixed quickly enough to prevent meaningful increases in catastrophic harm capability.

units.excerpt: Example techniques could include rapid vulnerability patching, the ability to escalate to law enforcement when appropriate, and any necessary retention of logs for these activities.
units.paraphrase: Examples include rapid patching, escalation to law enforcement, and log retention.

units.context_stem: To make the required showing, we will need to satisfy the following criteria:
units.excerpt: Monitoring: Prespecify empirical evidence that would show the system is operating within the accepted risk range and define a process for reviewing the system's performance on a reasonable cadence.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic must prespecify evidence showing the system operates within accepted risk range and define a regular review process.

units.excerpt: Process examples include monitoring responses to jailbreak bounties, doing historical analysis or background monitoring, and any necessary retention of logs for these activities.
units.paraphrase: Examples include monitoring jailbreak bounty responses, historical/background analysis, and log retention.

units.context_stem: To make the required showing, we will need to satisfy the following criteria:
units.excerpt: Trusted users: Establish criteria for determining when it may be appropriate to share a version of the model with reduced safeguards with trusted users.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic must set criteria for when sharing a reduced-safeguard model version with trusted users is appropriate.

units.excerpt: In addition, demonstrate that an alternative set of controls will provide equivalent levels of assurance. This could include a sufficient combination of user vetting, secure access controls, monitoring, log retention, and incident response protocols.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic must also show that alternative controls provide equivalent assurance, potentially combining vetting, access controls, monitoring, log retention, and incident response.

units.context_stem: To make the required showing, we will need to satisfy the following criteria:
units.excerpt: Third-party environments: Document how all relevant models will meet the criteria above, even if they are deployed in a third-party partner's environment that may have a different set of safeguards.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic must document how models meet these criteria even when deployed in third-party environments with different safeguards.

units.excerpt: When a model must meet the ASL-3 Security Standard, we will evaluate whether the measures we have implemented make us highly protected against most attackers' attempts at stealing model weights.
units.paraphrase: When the ASL-3 Security Standard applies, Anthropic will assess whether its measures provide strong protection against most weight-theft attempts.

units.excerpt: This criterion does not attempt to specify the exact red-teaming protocol (e.g., number of hours, level of access, or pass-fail criteria). Setting a principled pass-fail threshold will depend on other factors, such as the quality of our monitoring and ability to respond to jailbreaks rapidly.
units.paraphrase: The footnote clarifies that the red-teaming criterion does not fix a specific protocol, since a principled threshold depends on other factors like monitoring quality and response speed.

units.excerpt: Due to the likely ease of bypassing or removing safeguards via fine-tuning, it may be difficult or impossible for these red-teaming tests to pass if weights are released or if unmoderated fine-tuning access is provided to untrusted users.
units.paraphrase: The footnote notes that red-teaming tests may be difficult or impossible to pass if weights are released or unmoderated fine-tuning access is given to untrusted users, due to easy safeguard bypass via fine-tuning.

units.excerpt: We consider the following groups in scope: hacktivists, criminal hacker groups, organized cybercrime groups, terrorist organizations, corporate espionage teams, internal employees, and state-sponsored programs that use broad-based and non-targeted techniques (i.e., not novel attack chains).
units.paraphrase: Anthropic defines the in-scope threat actor groups for the ASL-3 Security Standard, including hacktivists, criminal groups, terrorists, insiders, and state actors using non-targeted techniques.

units.excerpt: The following groups are out of scope for the ASL-3 Security Standard because further testing (as discussed below) should confirm that the model would not meaningfully increase their ability to do harm: state-sponsored programs that specifically target us (e.g., through novel attack chains or insider compromise) and a small number (~10) of non-state actors with state-level resourcing or backing that are capable of developing novel attack chains that utilize 0-day attacks.
units.paraphrase: Certain highly sophisticated actors, including targeted state programs and about ten non-state actors with state-level resources, are excluded from ASL-3 Security Standard scope since further testing should confirm no meaningful harm increase.

units.excerpt: To make the required showing, we will need to satisfy the following criteria:
units.paraphrase: Anthropic states it must satisfy the following listed criteria to make the required showing for the Security Standard.

units.context_stem: To make the required showing, we will need to satisfy the following criteria:
units.excerpt: Threat modeling: Follow risk governance best practices, such as use of the MITRE ATT&CK Framework to establish the relationship between the identified threats, sensitive assets, attack vectors and, in doing so, sufficiently capture the resulting risks that must be addressed to protect model weights from theft attempts.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic must follow risk governance best practices, such as MITRE ATT&CK, to map threats, assets, and vectors and capture resulting weight-theft risks.

units.excerpt: As part of this requirement, we should specify our plans for revising the resulting threat model over time.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic should specify plans for revising the threat model over time.

units.context_stem: To make the required showing, we will need to satisfy the following criteria:
units.excerpt: Security frameworks: Align to and, as needed, extend industry-standard security frameworks for addressing identified risks, such as disclosure of sensitive information, tampering with accounts and assets, and unauthorized elevation of privileges with the appropriate controls.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic must align with, and extend as needed, industry-standard security frameworks to address risks like data disclosure, tampering, and privilege escalation.

units.excerpt: Perimeters and access controls: Building strong perimeters and access controls around sensitive assets to ensure AI models and critical systems are protected from unauthorized access.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic must build strong perimeters and access controls to protect models and critical systems from unauthorized access.

units.excerpt: We expect this will include a combination of physical security, encryption, cloud security, infrastructure policy, access management, and weight access minimization and monitoring.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic expects this to combine physical security, encryption, cloud security, infrastructure policy, access management, and weight access minimization/monitoring.

units.excerpt: Lifecycle security: Securing links in the chain of systems and software used to develop models, to prevent compromised components from being introduced and to ensure only trusted code and hardware is used.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic must secure the development chain to prevent compromised components and ensure only trusted code and hardware are used.

units.excerpt: We expect this will include a combination of software inventory, supply chain security, artifact integrity, binary authorization, hardware procurement, and secure research development lifecycle.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic expects this to combine software inventory, supply chain security, artifact integrity, binary authorization, hardware procurement, and secure R&D lifecycle practices.

units.excerpt: Monitoring: Proactively identifying and mitigating threats through ongoing and effective monitoring, testing for vulnerabilities, and laying traps for potential attackers.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic must proactively identify and mitigate threats via ongoing monitoring, vulnerability testing, and attacker traps.

units.excerpt: We expect this will include a combination of endpoint patching, product security testing, log management, asset monitoring, and intruder deception techniques.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic expects this to combine endpoint patching, product security testing, log management, asset monitoring, and deception techniques.

units.excerpt: Resourcing: Investing sufficient resources in security.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic must invest sufficient resources in security.

units.excerpt: We expect meeting this standard of security to require roughly 5-10% of employees being dedicated to security and security-adjacent work.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic expects that meeting this security standard requires roughly 5-10% of employees dedicated to security-related work.

units.excerpt: Existing guidance: Aligning where appropriate with existing guidance on securing model weights, including Securing AI Model Weights, Preventing Theft and Misuse of Frontier Models (2024); security recommendations like Deploying AI Systems Securely (CISA/NSA/FBI/ASD/CCCS/GCSB/GCHQ), ISO 42001, CSA's AI Safety Initiative, and CoSAI; and standards frameworks like SSDF, SOC 2, NIST 800-53.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic will align where appropriate with existing guidance and standards such as Securing AI Model Weights, Deploying AI Systems Securely, ISO 42001, CoSAI, SSDF, SOC 2, and NIST 800-53.

units.excerpt: We will implement robust controls to mitigate basic insider risk, but consider mitigating risks from sophisticated or state-compromised insiders to be out of scope for ASL-3.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic will implement robust controls for basic insider risk but excludes sophisticated or state-compromised insider risk from ASL-3 scope.

units.excerpt: We define "basic insider risk" as risk from an insider who does not have persistent or time-limited access to systems that process model weights.
units.paraphrase: The footnote defines basic insider risk as risk from an insider lacking persistent or time-limited access to weight-processing systems.

units.excerpt: We define "sophisticated insider risk" as risk from an insider who has persistent access or can request time-limited access to systems that process model weights.
units.paraphrase: The footnote defines sophisticated insider risk as risk from an insider with persistent or requestable time-limited access to weight-processing systems.

units.excerpt: We are committed to further enhancing these protections as a part of our ongoing preparations for higher security levels.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic commits to further enhancing insider risk protections as part of preparing for higher security levels.

units.context_stem: To make the required showing, we will need to satisfy the following criteria:
units.excerpt: Audits: Develop plans to (1) audit and assess the design and implementation of the security program and (2) share these findings (and updates on any remediation efforts) with management on an appropriate cadence.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic must develop plans to audit the security program and share findings and remediation updates with management regularly.

units.excerpt: We expect this to include independent validation of threat modeling and risk assessment results; a sampling-based audit of the operating effectiveness of the defined controls; periodic, broadly scoped, and independent testing with expert red-teamers who are industry-renowned and have been recognized in competitive challenges.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic expects audits to include independent validation of threat modeling and risk assessments, sampling-based control audits, and periodic independent testing by renowned expert red-teamers.

units.context_stem: To make the required showing, we will need to satisfy the following criteria:
units.excerpt: Third-party environments: Document how all relevant models will meet the criteria above, even if they are deployed in a third-party partner's environment that may have a different set of safeguards.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic must document how models meet security criteria even when deployed in third-party partner environments with different safeguards.

units.excerpt: If, after the evaluations above, we determine that we have met the ASL-3 Required Safeguards, then we may proceed with deploying and training models above the Capability Threshold, provided we have also conducted a follow-up capability assessment.
units.paraphrase: If Anthropic determines it has met the ASL-3 Required Safeguards, it may proceed with deployment and training above the Capability Threshold, contingent on a follow-up capability assessment.

units.excerpt: The process for determining whether we have met the ASL-3 Required Safeguards is as follows:
units.paraphrase: The following steps describe the process for determining whether ASL-3 Required Safeguards have been met.

units.context_stem: The process for determining whether we have met the ASL-3 Required Safeguards is as follows:
units.excerpt: First, we will compile a Safeguards Report for each Required Safeguard that documents our implementation of the measures above, makes an affirmative case for why we have satisfied them, and advances recommendations on deployment decisions.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic will first compile a Safeguards Report per Required Safeguard documenting implementation, arguing satisfaction, and recommending deployment decisions.

units.context_stem: The process for determining whether we have met the ASL-3 Required Safeguards is as follows:
units.excerpt: The Safeguards Report(s) will be escalated to the CEO and the Responsible Scaling Officer, who will (1) make the ultimate determination as to whether we have satisfied the Required Safeguards and (2) decide any deployment-related issues.
units.paraphrase: The Safeguards Report will go to the CEO and RSO, who will make the final determination on Required Safeguards satisfaction and decide deployment issues.

units.context_stem: The process for determining whether we have met the ASL-3 Required Safeguards is as follows:
units.excerpt: In general, as noted in Sections 7.1.4 and 7.2.2, we will solicit both internal and external expert feedback on the report as well as the CEO and RSO's conclusions to inform future refinements to our methodology.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic will generally solicit internal and external expert feedback on the report and the CEO/RSO conclusions to refine future methodology.

units.excerpt: For high-stakes issues, however, the CEO and RSO will likely solicit internal and external feedback on the report prior to making any decisions.
units.paraphrase: For high-stakes issues, the CEO and RSO will likely seek internal and external feedback before deciding.

units.context_stem: The process for determining whether we have met the ASL-3 Required Safeguards is as follows:
units.excerpt: If the CEO and RSO decide to proceed with deployment and training, they will share their decision–as well as the underlying Safeguards Report, internal feedback, and any external feedback–with the Board of Directors and the Long-Term Benefit Trust before moving forward.
units.paraphrase: If the CEO and RSO decide to proceed, they will share the decision, Safeguards Report, and feedback with the Board and Long-Term Benefit Trust before proceeding.

units.context_stem: The process for determining whether we have met the ASL-3 Required Safeguards is as follows:
units.excerpt: After the ASL-3 Required Safeguards are approved, they will be revisited and re-approved at least annually to re-affirm their suitability and sound implementation.
units.paraphrase: Once approved, ASL-3 Required Safeguards will be reviewed and re-approved at least once a year.

units.excerpt: If, however, we are unable to make the showing required above, we will restrict model deployment and further scaling.
units.paraphrase: If Anthropic cannot make the required showing, it will restrict deployment and further scaling of the model.

units.excerpt: In parallel with upgrading a model to the Required Safeguards, we will (1) update this policy to include any additional Capability Thresholds for which the Required Safeguards would be insufficient; and (2) conduct a follow-up capability assessment to determine that the model's capabilities fall sufficiently far away from those Capability Thresholds, following the procedures outlined in Section 3.
units.paraphrase: While upgrading a model's safeguards, Anthropic will update the policy for any new insufficient thresholds and conduct a follow-up capability assessment following Section 3 procedures.

units.excerpt: To summarize the commitments and procedures outlined above, we may deploy or store a model if either of the following criteria are met: (1) the model's capabilities are sufficiently far away from the existing Capability Thresholds, making the current ASL-2 Standard appropriate;
units.paraphrase: Anthropic may deploy or store a model if its capabilities are sufficiently far from existing Capability Thresholds, keeping ASL-2 appropriate.

units.excerpt: or (2) the model's capabilities have surpassed the existing Capabilities Threshold, but we have implemented the ASL-3 Required Safeguards and confirmed that the model is sufficiently far away from the next set of Capability Thresholds as to make the model ASL-3 Standard appropriate.
units.paraphrase: Or the model may be deployed if it has surpassed the existing threshold but ASL-3 Required Safeguards are implemented and confirmed sufficient relative to the next threshold set.

units.excerpt: We may also continue to train more capable models, conducting preliminary and comprehensive assessments as before.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic may continue training more capable models while conducting preliminary and comprehensive assessments as before.

units.excerpt: In any scenario where we determine that a model requires ASL-3 Required Safeguards but we are unable to implement them immediately, we will act promptly to reduce interim risk to acceptable levels until the ASL-3 Required Safeguards are in place:
units.paraphrase: If a model requires ASL-3 Required Safeguards that cannot be implemented immediately, Anthropic will act promptly to reduce interim risk to acceptable levels until safeguards are in place.

units.excerpt: Interim measures: The CEO and Responsible Scaling Officer may approve the use of interim measures that provide the same level of assurance as the relevant ASL-3 Standard but are faster or simpler to implement.
units.paraphrase: The CEO and RSO may approve interim measures providing equivalent assurance to the ASL-3 Standard but quicker or simpler to implement.

units.excerpt: In the deployment context, such measures might include blocking model responses, downgrading to a less-capable model in a particular domain, or increasing the sensitivity of automated monitoring.
units.paraphrase: Deployment-context interim measures might include blocking responses, downgrading to a less-capable model, or increasing monitoring sensitivity.

units.excerpt: In the security context, an example of such a measure would be storing the model weights in a single-purpose, isolated network that meets the ASL-3 Standard.
units.paraphrase: A security-context interim measure example is storing model weights in an isolated, single-purpose network meeting the ASL-3 Standard.

units.excerpt: In either case, the CEO and Responsible Scaling Officer will share their plan with the Board of Directors and the Long-Term Benefit Trust.
units.paraphrase: In either context, the CEO and RSO will share their interim measures plan with the Board and Long-Term Benefit Trust.

units.excerpt: Stronger restrictions: In the unlikely event that we cannot implement interim measures to adequately mitigate risk, we will impose stronger restrictions.
units.paraphrase: If interim measures cannot adequately mitigate risk, Anthropic will impose stronger restrictions.

units.excerpt: In the deployment context, we will de-deploy the model and replace it with a model that falls below the Capability Threshold. Once the ASL-3 Deployment Standard can be met, the model may be re-deployed.
units.paraphrase: In deployment, Anthropic will de-deploy the model and replace it with one below the Capability Threshold, allowing re-deployment once the ASL-3 Deployment Standard is met.

units.excerpt: In the security context, we will delete model weights. Given the availability of interim deployment and security protections, however, stronger restrictions should rarely be necessary.
units.paraphrase: In the security context, Anthropic will delete model weights, though stronger restrictions should rarely be needed given interim protections.

units.excerpt: Monitoring pretraining: We will not train models with comparable or greater capabilities to the one that requires the ASL-3 Security Standard.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic will not train models with capabilities comparable to or greater than one requiring the ASL-3 Security Standard.

units.excerpt: This is achieved by monitoring the capabilities of the model in pretraining and comparing them against the given model.
units.paraphrase: This is done by monitoring pretraining model capabilities and comparing them to the given model.

units.excerpt: If the pretraining model's capabilities are comparable or greater, we will pause training until we have implemented the ASL-3 Security Standard and established it is sufficient for the model.
units.paraphrase: If the pretraining model's capabilities are comparable or greater, Anthropic will pause training until the ASL-3 Security Standard is implemented and confirmed sufficient.

units.excerpt: We will set expectations with internal stakeholders about the potential for such pauses.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic will set expectations with internal stakeholders regarding the possibility of such training pauses.

units.excerpt: When choosing amongst options that satisfy the safety criteria, we will implement whichever interim safeguards minimize changes to customer experience.
units.paraphrase: Among safety-compliant options, Anthropic will implement whichever interim safeguards minimize customer experience changes.

units.excerpt: We consider implementation of the ASL-3 Security Standard alone sufficient to continue training, regardless of whether the ASL-3 Deployment Standard is satisfied.
units.paraphrase: The footnote states that implementing only the ASL-3 Security Standard suffices to continue training, regardless of the Deployment Standard's status.

units.excerpt: "Comparable or greater capabilities" is operationalized as 1x or more in Effective Compute.
units.paraphrase: The footnote defines "comparable or greater capabilities" as 1x or more Effective Compute.

units.context_stem: To facilitate the effective implementation of this policy across the company, we commit to the following:
units.excerpt: Responsible Scaling Officer: We will maintain the position of Responsible Scaling Officer, a designated member of staff who is responsible for reducing catastrophic risk, primarily by ensuring this policy is designed and implemented effectively.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic commits to maintaining a Responsible Scaling Officer role responsible for reducing catastrophic risk through effective policy design and implementation.

units.excerpt: The Responsible Scaling Officer's duties will include (but are not limited to): (1) as needed, proposing updates to this policy to the Board of Directors; (2) approving relevant model training or deployment decisions based on capability and safeguard assessments;
units.paraphrase: The RSO's duties include proposing policy updates and approving training/deployment decisions based on assessments.

units.excerpt: (3) reviewing major contracts (i.e., deployment partnerships) for consistency with this policy; (4) overseeing implementation of this policy, including the allocation of sufficient resources; (5) receiving and addressing reports of potential instances of noncompliance;
units.paraphrase: The RSO's duties also include reviewing major contracts, overseeing implementation and resource allocation, and handling noncompliance reports.

units.excerpt: (6) promptly notifying the Board of Directors of any cases of noncompliance that pose material risk; and (7) making judgment calls on policy interpretation and application.
units.paraphrase: The RSO's final duties are notifying the Board of material noncompliance and making interpretive judgment calls.

units.excerpt: Readiness: We will develop internal safety procedures for incident scenarios.
